questions.q: What do the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues and eigenvectors represent physically?
options: The eigenvalues are the system's possible energies, and the eigenvectors are the corresponding states of definite energy
The eigenvalues are measurement probabilities, and the eigenvectors are classical bit values
The eigenvalues represent time, and the eigenvectors represent position
The Hamiltonian has no physical interpretation beyond being a mathematical formality
questions.explain: As the energy observable, the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues are literally the possible energies a measurement could yield, and its eigenvectors are the states that have one of those energies with certainty.

questions.q: For H=(ħω/2)Z, what are the energy eigenstates and their corresponding eigenvalues?
options: |0⟩ with energy +ħω/2, and |1⟩ with energy −ħω/2
|+⟩ with energy +ħω/2, and |−⟩ with energy −ħω/2
Both |0⟩ and |1⟩ have the same energy, 0
There are no energy eigenstates for this Hamiltonian
questions.explain: Since Z|0⟩=|0⟩ and Z|1⟩=−|1⟩ (verified), multiplying by ħω/2 gives H|0⟩=(+ħω/2)|0⟩ and H|1⟩=(−ħω/2)|1⟩ -- |0⟩ and |1⟩ are the energy eigenstates, with eigenvalues ±ħω/2.

questions.q: Why do |0⟩'s measurement probabilities never change over time under this Hamiltonian, even though its state vector is technically evolving?
options: Because |0⟩ is an energy eigenstate, so time evolution only adds a global phase to it (verified in Lesson 26), and global phase doesn't affect measurement probabilities
Because |0⟩ never actually evolves under any Hamiltonian
Because measurement probabilities never change for any state, regardless of the Hamiltonian
Because |0⟩ has zero energy, so it is immune to the Schrödinger equation
questions.explain: Being an energy eigenstate means time evolution only multiplies |0⟩ by a phase factor e^(-iωt/2) -- a global phase, which is unobservable, so P(0) and P(1) stay fixed forever. This is exactly what 'stationary state' means.

questions.q: Why does |+⟩ develop an observable relative phase over time under H=(ħω/2)Z, while |0⟩ does not?
options: |+⟩ is a superposition of the two different-energy eigenstates |0⟩ and |1⟩, and their phases drift apart at different rates (ω/2 vs −ω/2), producing a relative phase between them over time
|+⟩ has no energy at all, so it cannot evolve under any Hamiltonian
|+⟩ and |0⟩ actually behave identically under this Hamiltonian
|+⟩ is itself an energy eigenstate of this Hamiltonian, just like |0⟩
questions.explain: Because |+⟩ mixes the +ħω/2 and −ħω/2 energy components, each picks up phase at a different rate, and that difference shows up as a genuine, physically observable relative phase -- exactly the mechanism verified numerically in Lesson 26.

questions.q: Why does the energy gap between a physical qubit's |0⟩ and |1⟩ states matter for real hardware?
options: The energy gap sets a physical control frequency for the qubit, which in turn constrains how fast gates can realistically be applied and how stable the qubit is
The energy gap has no real-world consequences; it only matters in abstract theoretical models
A larger energy gap always makes a qubit immune to all noise
The energy gap determines how many classical bits the qubit can store
questions.explain: The ħω energy gap corresponds to a real control frequency (e.g. a microwave or laser frequency used to drive the qubit), and this frequency sets real physical tradeoffs between gate speed and qubit stability in actual hardware.
